introduction:
logBD is a stream processing pipeline built to make sense of network email traffic at scale. FortiMail appliances produce continuous streams of log files, and logBD transforms those raw logs into a property graph — a queryable database of network entities and the relationships between them. The graph captures domains, hosts, subnets, URIs, email templates, and content clusters, along with how often they appear together in email traffic and what reputation signals they carry. The result is a live, continuously-updated picture of the network that analysts and automated systems can interrogate to identify spam infrastructure.

The platform serves two audiences. Security analysts use a REST API and CLI to look up individual entities, trace relationships, and investigate suspicious patterns. Automated ML classifiers use a high-throughput analytical interface to pull feature matrices across all known entities, run inference, and publish spam probability scores back into the graph. Both audiences query the same underlying data, but through interfaces tuned for their access patterns — point lookups for analysts, full table scans for the classifier.

logBD runs as approximately 32 pods on a single Kubernetes node, with each pipeline stage isolated in its own pod and its own storage file. This tight vertical deployment reflects the operational context: a single-site office network with known, bounded traffic volumes rather than a horizontally-scaled cloud service.
how_it_works:
Logs arrive as gzipped files written by FortiMail appliances to a shared network filesystem. A producer process watches for new time-slot directories, parses each log file into structured records, and publishes them to a message queue. From there, an extraction stage fans each message out into typed entity records — a single email log becomes separate records for the sending domain, host IP, URI paths, email template, and content cluster — which are routed to per-type queues consumed by dedicated storage workers. Each entity type has its own storage file and its own consumer process, so domains, hosts, and URIs accumulate independently without competing for the same write lock.

Once entities are stored, a separate computation layer periodically sweeps through them and enriches each record with derived analytical signals — traffic aggregations, reputation lookups, neighbor relationships, and graph-algorithm outputs — organized into tiers with refresh intervals ranging from five minutes to once-ever. The classifier then reads these enriched features through a high-throughput SQL interface, runs a LightGBM model to produce spam probability scores, and publishes those scores back to a dedicated queue where they are stored alongside external reference scores from services like FortiGuard. Analysts query the result through a REST API that serves entity lookups, graph traversals, and subgraph queries in under 50 milliseconds by maintaining warm connections to all storage files.
key_decisions: One storage file per entity type, one writer process per file. DuckDB holds exclusive file-level locks during writes, making shared writers impractical. Rather than working around this with a shared database, the architecture leans into it — each entity type gets its own isolated file and dedicated consumer, which simplifies concurrency reasoning and makes resource limits predictable at the cost of managing 27 separate files.

Two separate query interfaces for two different access patterns. The classifier needs to scan millions of rows to build feature matrices; the API needs to answer entity lookups in under 50ms. Routing full table scans through a shared session caused 150-400 second scan times on the largest tables. The architecture solves this by giving the classifier a gRPC analytical SQL interface and giving the API direct connections to individual snapshot files — the same data, two different paths.

Subprocess isolation for ML jobs. Each classifier job (inference, training, dataset preparation) runs as a subprocess rather than in-process. This means Python fully reclaims memory between runs, preventing the memory growth typical in long-running ML pipelines. Job state is persisted to disk with atomic writes so the scheduler can resume cleanly after a crash.

groups_overview.name: Ingestion
groups_overview.role: Watches for new log files on the network filesystem, parses them into structured records, and routes individual entity types to separate message queues.

groups_overview.name: Graph Engine
groups_overview.role: Consumes entity records from queues and persists them to storage, then periodically enriches stored entities with analytical signals computed in tiers.

groups_overview.name: Query Layer
groups_overview.role: Serves entity lookups, graph traversals, and SQL queries to analysts, CLI users, LLM agents, and the classifier through four distinct interfaces.

groups_overview.name: Classification
groups_overview.role: Runs ML inference on enriched entity features on a 30-minute cycle, retrains models weekly, and publishes spam probability scores back into the graph.
